issues.failure_explanation: The proof bounds the weighted residual of (u_ε,f_ε) by P times norms of û=u−u_ε and f̂, which implicitly uses that the weighted residual of the exact pair (u,f) vanishes. This holds only when all weights in a residual coincide. For general bounded weights (e.g. φ_{θ^1}≡2, all others ≡1, or φ_{θ^6}≡2, φ_{θ^7}≡1) one has φ_{θ^1}∂_t u−Σφ̄_i∂_{ii}u+φ_{θ^2}v(u)−φ_{θ^3}f1_ω=∂_t u≠0 and φ_{θ^6}u(0)−φ_{θ^7}u_0=u_0≠0, so the weighted losses of (u,f) are bounded below by fixed positive quantities (e.g. |Q_T|^{-1}‖∂_t u‖²−ρ|Q_T|), which can exceed any bound tending to 0 as W,L→∞, δ→0. The trace bound ‖R̄_Γ^1(u_θ)‖≤P‖u_θ−u‖_{H^1(Γ)}/√|Γ| likewise ignores the terms (φ_{θ^6}−φ_{θ^7})u_0, (φ_{θ^8}−φ_{θ^9})z_0. The theorem's 'any parameters' quantifier is therefore false.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict Theorems 3.1–3.2 and 3.5–3.6 to weights that coincide within each residual (φ_{θ^1}=φ̄_i=φ_{θ^2}=φ_{θ^3}, φ_{θ^6}=φ_{θ^7}, φ_{θ^8}=φ_{θ^9}, etc., in particular the standard-PINN case φ≡1), and drop the 'any parameters' claim.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed guarantee that the WeightedPINN loss can be made arbitrarily small for any choice of weight networks (all four approximation theorems) is false; only the special case of identical (e.g. ≡1, standard PINN) weights survives.
issues.title: Weighted residual of the exact controlled solution does not vanish for arbitrary weights; approximation theorems false as stated
issues.why_classification: The central quantifier of the WeightedPINN approximation result must be abandoned; no version covering general adaptive weights survives, leaving essentially only the standard PINN statement.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: It follows from the approach developed in \cite{Cazenave1980} (see also \cite[Equation (1.4)]{FernandezZuazua2000}) that the above semilinear heat equation admits a unique solution. Consequently, \(\bar u\) is well defined.

issues.failure_explanation: ū is defined as the solution of the heat equation ∂_t ū−Δū+v(ū)=f_θ̄1_ω with terminal datum ū(T)=z_0, i.e. a backward heat problem, which is ill-posed (no solution exists for general z_0∈L²(Ω), and the cited well-posedness results concern the forward Cauchy problem). Moreover, the energy inequality ∂_t‖û‖²+‖û‖²_{H¹}≤C_0(‖û‖²+…) is a forward differential inequality; integrating it from t to T yields ‖û(t)‖²≥‖û(T)‖²−C_0∫_t^T(…), a lower bound, not the stated upper bound ‖û(t)‖²≤e^{C_0(T−t)}(‖û(T)‖²+…). Thus \eqref{eq:hat_u_est1} is unproved.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Define ū as the forward solution with ū(0)=u_0 (well-posed), run the energy estimate forward in time to bound u_θ−ū by the loss, and restructure the subsequent control-comparison step accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The state-error estimate \eqref{eq:hat_u_est1} and hence the conclusion of Theorem 3.3 are unsupported; the wave analogue is not affected by this root (time reversibility).
issues.title: Comparison solution defined via an ill-posed backward semilinear heat equation and Grönwall applied in the wrong time direction
issues.why_classification: Fixing this requires replacing the comparison construction and rewriting the energy argument (a contained replacement argument), but does not by itself require new global architecture.

issues.failure_explanation: The energy identity produces the boundary flux ∫_{∂Ω}u_θ(∇u_θ·ν). The normal derivative ∇u_θ·ν is not part of the H¹(∂Ω) (or H¹(Σ_T)) norm, which only contains tangential and time derivatives, so ‖∇u_θ·ν‖_{L²(∂Ω)}≤‖u_θ‖_{H¹(∂Ω)} is false. Furthermore, the weighted boundary residual \eqref{eq:barRG1} with φ≡1 contains only ‖u_θ‖_{L²(Σ_T)} and ‖∂_t u_θ‖_{L²(Σ_T)} (no spatial derivatives at all), so it does not even reduce to ‖u_θ‖²_{H¹(Σ_T)} as the proof asserts. Hence the loss bound ≤δ gives no control of the flux term, and \eqref{eq:hat_u_est1} (and its wave analogue, where ∫_{∂Ω}∂_t u_θ(∇u_θ·ν) appears) is not implied by the hypothesis.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Redefine the boundary residuals (both standard and weighted, e.g. include ‖φ_{θ̃^i}∂_{x_i}u_θ‖_{L²(Σ_T)} for all i as in Section 2.3) so that the full gradient of u_θ on Σ_T is penalized, and use that term to bound the flux; adjust the trace step in the approximation theorems accordingly (H²(Q_T) traces suffice).
issues.overall_effect: The error estimates of Theorems 3.3 and 3.4 do not follow from smallness of the defined losses; the reduction 'WeightedPINN with φ≡1 = standard PINN' is also inaccurate for the boundary term.
issues.title: Boundary flux term in energy estimate is not controlled by the loss (normal derivative absent from H¹(Σ_T) and from the weighted boundary residual)
issues.why_classification: Requires modifying the loss definitions and the corresponding proof steps, but a recognizably identical result is recovered with a contained change.

issues.failure_explanation: Controllability theorems assert the existence of some control with norm bounded by the data; they do not bound an arbitrary given control steering the same data (null controls are highly non-unique). The proof applies the bound to the specific control f−f_θ̄, which is unjustified. The conclusion is in fact false: if (u',f') is any other exact controlled pair for \eqref{Heat1} with f'≠f, then networks approximating (u',f') drive the loss to 0 while ‖f−f_θ̄‖ and ‖u−u_θ‖ stay bounded away from 0, contradicting ‖f−f_θ̄‖²≤Cδ for all δ. The same misapplication occurs in \eqref{eq:f_est2} for the wave equation.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The domain \(\omega\subset\Omega\) contains a neighborhood of the boundary \(\partial \Omega\).

issues.failure_explanation: With d=10 the center (1/d,…,1/d) has norm 1/√10≈0.316, so its distance to ∂Ω (unit sphere) is ≈0.684<3/4; the closed ball of radius 3/4 thus meets ∂Ω, and ω=Ω∖(ball) cannot contain a neighborhood of ∂Ω. The claim that (A3) is satisfied (and the added assumption that ω contains ∂Ω) is inconsistent with the stated geometry.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Shrink the radius (e.g. below 1−1/√d) or move the center so that the excluded ball is compactly contained in Ω, or drop the claim that (A3) holds.
